source_caption:
Tom Hanks agreed to star in Forrest Gump (1994) after reading the script for about an hour and a half. One of his main conditions was that the story stay historically believable and grounded, even with its fictional elements.

During production, Robert Zemeckis ran into major budget problems when Paramount Pictures cut around $10 million from the budget. The studio pushed him to remove expensive scenes, including parts involving the shrimp boat and the Vietnam sequences. Zemeckis fought hard to keep those moments because they were essential to the story. To help save the film’s scale, both he and Hanks agreed to give up part of their upfront salaries in exchange for a percentage of the profits, a risky move that paid off later when Hanks reportedly earned around $70 million from the film’s success.

One of the most famous parts of the movie, Forrest’s long running journey across America, was almost cut as well. Zemeckis officially agreed to reduce it but quietly filmed much of the sequence anyway, with some behind the scenes support from production executive Michelle Manning. Many of the wide running shots were done by Tom Hanks’ younger brother, Jim Hanks, because he could copy Forrest’s unique, slightly awkward running style better than other stunt doubles.

When the studio finally saw the footage, they approved the scenes after realizing how important they were to the film. One iconic shot, filmed in Monument Valley, wasn’t funded by the studio at all, so Hanks and Zemeckis ended up paying for it themselves to make sure the moment stayed in the movie.

source_details.title: Forrest Gump
source_details.synopsis: Forrest Gump is a 1994 American comedy-drama film directed by Robert Zemeckis. An adaptation of the 1986 novel of the same name by Winston Groom, the film's screenplay was written by Eric Roth. It stars Tom Hanks in the title role, alongside Robin Wright, Gary Sinise, Mykelti Williamson, and Sally Field in lead roles. The film follows the life of an Alabama man named Forrest Gump (Hanks) and his experiences in the 20th-century United States. Principal photography took place between August and December 1993, mainly in the tri-states Georgia, North Carolina, and South Carolina.
